title: From term sheet to commitment: what a construction lender actually promises
summary: A construction loan moves through three documents: a term sheet that binds almost nothing, a commitment letter that binds the lender only if conditions are met, and a loan agreement that sets the conditions, covenants and events of default you will live under for the whole build. This lesson teaches what each stage promises and what has to be true before a single dollar is advanced.
body:
A construction lender does not promise to lend you money. It promises to lend you money if a long list of things is true on the day you ask, and it keeps the right to stop if other things become true later. Learn the list and you can plan the build around it; ignore it and the money stops when you need it most.

Recall

Q. In a waterfall, what is a clawback?

A. An obligation on the sponsor to return promote already received if, at the end of the deal, investors have not received their capital and preferred return. It is only worth something if it is backed by escrow or a guarantee from someone with assets.

Q. What is the attachment point of a layer in the capital stack?

A. The level of value, as a percentage of cost or value, below which that layer starts to lose money.

Q. What is highest and best use?

A. The use of a site that is legally permitted, physically possible, financially feasible and produces the highest value. It is the starting point for valuing land.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a stabilised building has income to pay its loan. A construction project has none: it has a budget, a schedule and a promise. The construction lender is funding a building that does not yet exist, so it protects itself with conditions rather than with income. Every condition is a date and a document you must produce. A developer who treats the commitment letter as the finish line discovers that funding the first draw is a second negotiation, conducted with his equity already spent.

Three documents, three levels of promise

The term sheet is a short summary of proposed terms: amount, rate, fees, sizing tests, security and key conditions. In most markets it states expressly that it is not a commitment to lend, apart from a few binding clauses such as confidentiality, exclusivity and the borrower's promise to pay the lender's costs. It is an invitation to spend money on diligence.

The commitment letter comes after the lender's credit committee approves the loan. It is the lender's written undertaking to lend on stated terms, subject to stated conditions, and it usually expires if the loan is not documented and closed by a date. The borrower normally signs it and pays a commitment fee. Whether it binds, and to what extent, depends on its wording and the governing law, which we study on day four.

The loan agreement is the full contract. It sets out when the lender must fund, what you promise throughout the build, and what entitles the lender to stop. Three families of terms do most of the work.

Conditions precedent: what must be true to get paid

A condition precedent (CP) is something that must be satisfied before the lender is obliged to act. Construction loans have three sets. Conditions to signing or closing: corporate authorisations, title, the security registered, insurance, legal opinions. Conditions to the first draw, usually the heaviest: the building permit, the construction contract signed, the budget and schedule approved by the lender's monitor, environmental and geotechnical reports, any pre-leasing or pre-sales the term sheet required, and, critically, the borrower's equity contributed in full. Conditions to every draw: no default continuing, representations still true, the loan still in balance, and the monitor's certificate of work in place.

Here is the first worked example. A hypothetical project costs 30,000,000 dollars. The loan is 65 percent of cost, 19,500,000, and the equity is 10,500,000. The commitment letter expires in 90 days. The CP list includes the building permit, which the planning office says will take 120 days. On those facts the commitment will lapse 30 days before the permit can exist. Either you negotiate an outside date of at least 150 days before you sign, or you are paying a commitment fee for a promise you cannot use. The professional habit is a CP tracker: every condition, its owner, its lead time, and the date it is needed, built backward from the first draw.

Say that out loud now.

Covenants: what you promise while the money is out

Covenants are continuing promises. Positive covenants require you to do things: build in line with the approved plans and budget, deliver monthly reports, keep insurance in force, and complete by an outside date. Negative covenants forbid things: no other debt, no sale or transfer of the project or change of control, no changes to the construction contract above a threshold without consent. Financial covenants, which matter more after completion, may include a minimum net worth or liquidity for the guarantor during the build.

The second worked example is the completion covenant. Suppose the schedule shows completion in 22 months and the loan's outside completion date is month 24. A three-month delay puts you in breach in month 25. Two months of float sounds comfortable until you remember that construction schedules slip routinely. Negotiate the outside date against a sober schedule, with an extension right on payment of a fee, rather than discovering in month 23 that extension is entirely at the lender's discretion.

Events of default: what lets the lender stop

An event of default is a listed occurrence that entitles the lender to exercise remedies: stop funding, demand immediate repayment, take over the project and enforce its security. The usual list is non-payment, breach of covenant after any cure period, a representation proving untrue, insolvency of the borrower or guarantor, failure to complete by the outside date, abandonment of the works, and cross-default, meaning a default under another loan triggering this one. Some lists include a material adverse change: a broad catch-all that the lender may invoke if something significantly worsens the project or the borrower.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners treat the commitment letter as the start of a project, not the end of a negotiation. A single named person owns the CP tracker and reviews it weekly with the lawyer and the project manager. The budget, schedule and construction contract are finalised before the commitment letter is signed, so the lender's conditions reflect the real project. And every event of default is mapped to a cure path: who would know first, what they would do, and how long they have. A small developer can copy all three with a spreadsheet and a standing weekly call.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is spending your equity before every condition to the first draw is certain, so the project depends on a lender that has not yet become obliged to fund. The control is to sequence equity spending against the CP tracker, and to hold back irreversible commitments until the critical conditions are satisfied or clearly on track.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a signed commitment letter means the money is secured. It means the money is available if every condition is met in time, and the lender decides whether they are.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: commitment, standby and arrangement fees may be treated as capitalised project cost or as finance expense, which changes when the deduction arrives; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: construction loans commonly add completion and cost-overrun guarantees, so read them as part of the loan. Banking: every event of default, including cross-default, can stop funding mid-build. Governance: the borrowing, the security and each guarantee need proper resolutions, and the negative covenants limit what the board may later decide alone. Estate: a guarantor's death or incapacity can itself be an event of default, so plan succession of guarantees. Exit: the change-of-control covenant restricts selling the project company before completion without consent.

Callback

In week 31 we learned desk diligence: legal, environmental and geotechnical questions answered before committing to land. Those same reports reappear here as conditions precedent to the first draw. Diligence done well at acquisition shortens the CP list later; diligence skipped at acquisition becomes the condition that delays your loan.

Recap

The term sheet invites diligence, the commitment letter promises funding subject to conditions, and the loan agreement sets conditions precedent, covenants and events of default. Build a CP tracker backward from the first draw, negotiate dates against a sober schedule, and map every default to a cure path.

Next: Ford, with Roman, takes Dubai World through failure forensics: development debt, a standstill request and the reach of a default.
checklist: List every condition precedent by stage: closing, first draw, every draw
Build the CP tracker backward from the first draw date
Compare each CP lead time with the commitment expiry
Negotiate the outside completion date against a sober schedule
Secure an extension right on payment of a fee
Map every event of default to who knows first and the cure path
Hold back irreversible spending until critical CPs are certain
Run the Six-Lens Check before signing the commitment letter
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, construction lending in one minute. The lender is funding a building that does not exist, so it protects itself with conditions instead of income. The term sheet binds almost nothing. The commitment letter promises to lend on stated terms if stated conditions are met, and it expires on a date. The loan agreement sets three families of terms. Conditions precedent must be true before funding: at closing, at the first draw, and at every draw, including my equity spent in full. Covenants are what I promise during the build, such as completing by an outside date. Events of default let the lender stop funding and demand repayment, including cross-default from another loan. On a 30,000,000 dollar project with a 90-day commitment and a 120-day permit, the commitment lapses before the permit exists. So I build a CP tracker backward from the first draw and negotiate dates against a sober schedule.
terms: Commitment letter — a lender's written undertaking, after credit approval, to lend on stated terms subject to stated conditions and an expiry date.
Condition precedent (CP) — a requirement that must be satisfied before a party is obliged to perform, such as before a lender must fund.
Event of default — a listed occurrence that entitles the lender to stop funding, demand repayment and enforce its security.

hostile.q: Your commitment expires in 90 days and your permit takes 120. How do you close?
hostile.a: We will not sign on those dates. I am asking for an outside date of 150 days with one 30-day extension on payment of a fee, and the permit is the only condition on the critical path. Every other CP is tracked weekly with an owner, and our equity spending is sequenced so nothing irreversible is committed before the permit issues.

title: Dubai World: development debt, a standstill and the reach of a default
summary: In November 2009 the Dubai government-owned conglomerate Dubai World asked its creditors for a standstill on its debts, after a property boom financed largely with borrowing ended. Ford, with Roman, takes the case through seven steps and finds the root cause in funding long developments with debt that had to be refinanced, and in creditors' faith in support that was never written down.
rule: Rule 39: I never fund a long build with debt that matures or can be called before the project can repay it, and I map every cross-default so that one failure cannot pull down the rest.
body:
Dubai World did not run out of land or ambition. It ran out of time on its debt: borrowing that had to be repaid or refinanced long before the developments it funded could pay for themselves, in a market that stopped lending all at once.

Recall

Q. What is a condition precedent in a construction loan?

A. Something that must be true before the lender is obliged to fund, such as the building permit, the signed construction contract, or the borrower's equity fully contributed.

Q. What does an intercreditor standstill do?

A. It stops one lender from enforcing for an agreed period while another tries to cure the problem.

Q. Why does a promote need a clawback?

A. Because promote paid on early profits can turn out to be unearned once the whole deal is counted, and investors need a way to recover it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the facts below are the broad public outline; check the dates and details against reliable sources before you rely on them, and treat any figure you meet elsewhere as needing verification. The case matters because its mechanics apply at any scale. A small developer with two construction loans and a land loan can suffer exactly the same chain: a maturity that cannot be refinanced, a default that crosses into the other loans, and creditors discovering that the support they assumed was never promised. Roman assists because this is the lender's view of development risk.

Step 1: the timeline

Through the early and mid 2000s Dubai experienced a rapid property boom, helped by rules that allowed foreign buyers to own freehold property in designated areas. Large master-planned developments, including artificial islands, were launched by government-linked developers, among them Nakheel, a subsidiary of Dubai World. Many projects were sold off-plan, with buyers paying instalments during construction. Funding came heavily from bank loans and bonds, much of it with maturities shorter than the developments themselves. In 2008 the global financial crisis closed credit markets and Dubai property prices fell sharply from their peak. On 25 November 2009, Dubai World announced it would ask creditors for a standstill on its debt. Markets reacted sharply. In December 2009 Abu Dhabi provided support that allowed a Nakheel Islamic bond, a sukuk, to be repaid when due. In 2010 Dubai World agreed a restructuring with its bank creditors that extended maturities.

Step 2: the key decisions

Three decisions stand out. Funding multi-year master developments with debt that had to be repaid or rolled over within a few years. Relying on continuing off-plan sales and rising prices to fund construction. And, on the creditors' side, lending on the assumption of state support rather than on the project's own ability to repay.

Step 3: the assumptions

The borrower assumed refinancing would always be available, because it always had been. Buyers would keep paying instalments, because prices kept rising. Creditors assumed that a government-owned company would be supported in full if needed. When the government made clear it had not guaranteed Dubai World's debts, that last assumption became visible as an assumption.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: the incentives

Developers were rewarded for launching and selling quickly, because off-plan deposits funded the next project. Lenders and bond investors were rewarded with fees and spreads, and comforted by perceived state backing, so they had little reason to insist on maturities matched to completion. Buyers were rewarded by rising prices for buying early and selling before completion. Everyone's incentive pointed towards more volume and shorter funding.

Step 5: the warning signs ignored

Credit markets froze in 2008, a year before the standstill request. Property prices were falling. Off-plan buyers in a falling market stop paying, which removes the cash flow that construction depended on. And large maturities were visible in advance on the borrowing schedule. None of these signs was hidden.

Step 6: the point of no return

The point of no return was the arrival of large maturities in a market that would not refinance them. Until then, assets could be sold, projects slowed or equity raised. Once debt fell due with markets shut and prices down, the only paths were outside support or a negotiated standstill and restructuring.

Step 7: the root cause

The root cause was a maturity mismatch: long, illiquid developments funded with shorter debt that depended on refinancing and continuing sales. The faith in unwritten support allowed the mismatch to grow. Roman's lender view: if a loan only works because someone not party to it might step in, it is not a loan to the project, it is a bet on the bystander.

What it means for a construction loan

Bring it down to a hypothetical scale. A developer has three loans: a land loan of 4,000,000 dollars maturing in 18 months, a construction loan of 20,000,000 on a second project maturing in 30 months, and a third construction loan of 15,000,000 just signed. All three contain cross-default clauses: a default under any other debt of the borrower group is a default under this one. The land loan cannot be refinanced at maturity because land values have fallen. That single payment default crosses into both construction loans. The construction lenders may stop funding mid-build, even though both projects are on budget. One maturity has frozen 35,000,000 dollars of construction funding.

The second worked example measures the mismatch. If the third project takes 26 months to build and 6 months to sell out, it needs 32 months from first draw to repayment. A loan maturing at 30 months leaves it two months short in the base case, and any delay widens the gap. The mismatch is visible on day one, in the arithmetic, before anyone has broken ground.

What a lender would test today

Roman's practical translation for a lender reading your file. First, it lays every maturity in your group on one timeline against each project's delayed completion and sale. Second, it asks who, by name and by signed document, would support the borrower if a refinancing failed; if the answer is "the market" or "a related party who has always helped", it treats that support as zero. Third, it reads the cross-default clause in every other loan you have, because those clauses decide whether its own loan is safe from your other lenders. A borrower who has already done all three, and can show the timeline on one page, is a borrower the lender can approve quickly. A borrower who has not is asking the lender to make the same assumption Dubai World's creditors made.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a maturity, anywhere in your group, that arrives before the asset it funds can repay it. The control is a single maturity schedule for every loan you are party to, tested against a delayed completion, with no maturity inside the delayed timeline unless an extension right is already written into the loan.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads cross-default as a clause about other people's loans. It is about yours: the weakest loan in your group sets the risk of all of them.

The prevention rule

Rule 39: I never fund a long build with debt that matures or can be called before the project can repay it, and I map every cross-default so that one failure cannot pull down the rest.

Callback

In week 27 we studied cycles: credit tightens before prices fall, and both happen faster than development timelines. Dubai World is that lesson at full scale. Your debt timeline must survive the cycle turning halfway through your build, because sometimes it does.

Recap

Long developments were funded with shorter debt that relied on refinancing, rising prices and unwritten support. When credit froze and prices fell, maturities arrived with nowhere to go, and a standstill followed. Match maturities to a delayed timeline and map every cross-default.

Next: Priya on the money: what conditions, fees and equity-first funding cost, and how delay in satisfying them eats your return.
checklist: Build one maturity schedule for every loan in the group
Test each maturity against a delayed completion and sale
Require extension rights for any maturity inside the delayed timeline
List every cross-default clause and the debts it reaches
Ring-fence each project in its own borrower where lenders allow
Never rely on support from anyone not party to the loan
Watch credit market conditions as a warning sign, not just prices
State Rule 39 before signing any new facility
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, Dubai World in one minute. During a property boom, government-linked developers in Dubai funded large, long developments with bank loans and bonds that matured sooner than the projects could repay them, relying on off-plan sales, rising prices and refinancing. In 2008 credit markets froze and prices fell. In November 2009 Dubai World asked creditors for a standstill, and creditors learned that the state support many had assumed had never been written down. A restructuring followed in 2010. The root cause was a maturity mismatch. At small scale, a developer whose land loan cannot be refinanced can trigger cross-default in two construction loans and freeze funding on projects that are on budget. Rule 39: I never fund a long build with debt that matures or can be called before the project can repay it, and I map every cross-default.
terms: Standstill — an agreement or request that creditors refrain from enforcing their claims for a period while a debt is renegotiated.
Maturity mismatch — funding a long-lived asset with debt that must be repaid or refinanced before the asset can repay it.
Cross-default — a clause making a default under another debt of the borrower or its group a default under this loan.

hostile.q: Your land loan matures before your construction loan's first draw. What stops a cross-default freezing everything?
hostile.a: I will not close the construction loan on those terms. Before signing, the land loan will be extended past the delayed first draw date or repaid from equity, and the construction loan's cross-default will be limited to debts of the project borrower above a set amount, not to every debt in my group. The maturity schedule for all three facilities is attached.

title: What the conditions cost: fees, equity first and the price of delay
summary: Construction loan conditions cost money in three ways: fees paid to obtain and hold the commitment, the return lost by putting all equity in before any debt, and the carrying cost of every month the conditions take. This lesson puts numbers on each, adds Warrick's Wealth Ledger on locked-up personal cash, and opens the monthly thread on decision journals.
body:
A construction loan's headline rate is only part of its cost. The fees to hold the commitment, the requirement that your equity goes in first, and the carrying cost of every month spent satisfying conditions can together move your return by more than a quarter-point change in the rate.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the Dubai World case?

A. A maturity mismatch: long developments funded with shorter debt that depended on refinancing, rising prices and support that was never written down.

Q. What does preferred equity usually behave like, despite its name?

A. Expensive debt with a control switch: a promised return, a repayment date and a right to remove the manager.

Q. What does desk diligence on a site cover before purchase?

A. Legal, tax, environmental and geotechnical questions answered from records and reports, so the price reflects known risks before money is committed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two term sheets with the same rate can differ in cost by hundreds of thousands of dollars once fees, funding order and timing are counted. If you compare only rates, you will pick the wrong lender as often as the right one. All figures are hypothetical, and fee levels are commercial practice that varies by lender and market, not a standard.

The fees

Construction loans commonly carry an arrangement or commitment fee paid at signing or closing, a fee on the undrawn balance while the loan is being drawn down, an exit fee on repayment in some markets, and the lender's own legal and monitoring costs, which the borrower pays.

The first worked example. A hypothetical loan of 19,500,000 dollars charges an arrangement fee of 1 percent, 195,000, at closing. During the build, the undrawn balance averages about 10,000,000 for 18 months, and a standby fee of 0.5 percent a year on undrawn amounts costs about 75,000. Lender's legal costs at closing, say 120,000, and monthly monitoring visits of 5,000 for 22 months, 110,000. Total: about 500,000 dollars, or about 2.6 percent of the loan, before a single dollar of interest. Compare that with a competing offer at a rate a quarter-point higher but half the fees, and the cheaper rate may be the dearer loan.

Equity first: the cost of going first

Most construction lenders require the borrower's entire equity to be spent before the first draw, so the lender's money is never the first to be lost. The alternative, rarely offered to smaller developers, is pro rata funding, where equity and debt fund each invoice in proportion.

The second worked example shows why it matters to return. The project costs 30,000,000 dollars, with 10,500,000 of equity and 19,500,000 of debt, and costs are spent evenly over 24 months, 1,250,000 a month. With equity first, the 10,500,000 is gone by about month 8.4, and debt funds the remaining 15.6 months. With pro rata funding, each month's 1,250,000 is split 35 percent equity, 65 percent debt, so equity goes in at about 437,500 a month across all 24 months. The total equity is the same. But under equity first, the average dollar of equity is invested about 20 months before completion; under pro rata, about 12 months before. Holding the profit constant, equity first means your money is tied up longer, which lowers your internal rate of return even though the equity multiple is unchanged.

Equity first does reduce interest, because debt is drawn later. That partly offsets the IRR effect. The honest comparison runs both cases through the cash flow and compares IRR and total cost, not one or the other.

Say that out loud now.

The price of delay

Every month between buying land and the first draw costs money: land loan interest, property taxes, insurance, professional fees and the return your equity is not earning. Conditions precedent decide how many of those months you pay for.

Take a land loan of 4,000,000 dollars at a hypothetical 8 percent: about 26,700 dollars of interest a month. Add property taxes, insurance and design team retainers of, say, 20,000 a month. A three-month delay in satisfying one condition, such as a missing environmental report or a construction contract still under negotiation, costs about 140,000 dollars directly. If the commitment expires and must be renewed, add a renewal fee. If the delay pushes construction into a season with higher costs, add that too. Delay is rarely the loan's fault; it is usually the borrower's CP tracker that started too late.

How the best do it

Experienced developers price a construction loan on total cost of funds across the whole build, not on the margin. They model each offer as a full cash flow including fees, funding order and expected draw timing, and compare the resulting IRR and total finance cost side by side. They also negotiate fees and conditions together: an extra condition the lender wants can be traded for a lower fee, because both are the lender's protection.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view of the personal balance sheet. Equity first means your cash leaves your control early and stays locked in an illiquid project for the whole build, often two years or more, with no distributions. Before committing, count that cash out of your available liquidity from the day it is spent, not from the day of completion, and check that your liquidity floor survives the full build plus a delay. If you are also giving a completion or cost-overrun guarantee, the lender will often test your liquidity and net worth as a covenant, so the same cash cannot be counted twice. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Decision journals

This month's thread is the decision journal. When you accept a fee, a condition or a funding order, write one paragraph the same day: what you chose, the alternatives, the numbers you relied on, and what you expect to happen. It takes five minutes.

The value appears two years later, when the project is complete. You can compare what you expected with what happened, and see whether your judgment about lenders, timelines and costs is improving or merely confident. Without the journal, memory quietly rewrites every decision as one you always knew was right.

One more cost belongs on the list: the rate lock. If a lender fixes or caps the rate at commitment but the loan closes months later, it may charge for holding that rate, or pass on the cost of a hedge bought early. Ask whether the rate is set at commitment, at closing or at each draw, and what it costs to hold it until the conditions are met.

Finally, ask which costs the lender treats as eligible. If a developer fee or interest on your own equity is excluded from the cost base, the loan-to-cost test is calculated on a smaller number and your required equity rises before you have spent a dollar.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a lender on margin alone and discovering that fees, equity-first funding and conditions cost more than the margin saved. The control is a full cash-flow comparison of every offer, including fees, funding order and a realistic first-draw date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the months before the first draw as free. They are the most expensive months of the project, because they carry cost with no progress.

Callback

In week 15 we learned that IRR rewards speed and the equity multiple does not. Equity first is that lesson in action: the same equity and the same profit produce a lower IRR because the money goes in sooner. Always report both measures when comparing funding structures.

Recap

Count every fee as a percentage of the loan. Model equity first against pro rata as full cash flows. Price each month of delay before first draw. Lock personal cash out of your liquidity from the day it is spent, and write down why you chose each term.

Next: LEX on the rules: what makes a commitment letter binding, how conditions and defaults are read, and how Canada and Guyana approach enforcement.
checklist: List every fee and express the total as a percentage of the loan
Model each offer as a full cash flow including fees and draw timing
Compare equity-first and pro rata funding on IRR and total cost
Price each month of delay before the first draw
Trade extra lender conditions for lower fees
Remove locked equity from personal liquidity from the day it is spent
Check guarantor liquidity covenants against the same cash
Record each funding decision in a decision journal the same day
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the cost of conditions in one minute. On a hypothetical 19,500,000 dollar construction loan, an arrangement fee, a standby fee on undrawn amounts, the lender's legal costs and monthly monitoring add up to about 500,000, roughly 2.6 percent of the loan, before interest. Equity first means all 10,500,000 of my equity goes in before the first draw, so each equity dollar is tied up about 20 months instead of 12 under pro rata funding. Same profit, lower IRR, partly offset by less interest. Every month before first draw costs land interest, taxes and fees; on a 4,000,000 land loan, a three-month delay costs about 140,000. So I compare lenders on full cash flows, not margin. I count locked equity out of my liquidity from the day it is spent, and I record every funding decision in a journal the same day.
terms: Standby fee — a fee charged on the undrawn portion of a committed loan while it is available.
Equity first — a requirement that the borrower's entire equity be spent on the project before the lender advances any loan funds.
Pro rata funding — funding each cost in fixed proportions from equity and debt throughout the build.

hostile.q: Our margin is a quarter-point higher than the other lender's. Why would you choose us?
hostile.a: Because I compared total cost, not margin. The other offer carries about 500,000 of fees and requires equity first; yours has lower fees and lets us fund the last 20 percent of equity pro rata. Across the full cash flow, your loan costs about 90,000 less in total finance cost and raises our IRR, so the higher margin is the cheaper loan.

title: How the promise is read: binding commitments, conditions and defaults
summary: Whether a commitment letter binds, how conditions are interpreted, and what happens after an event of default are questions of contract law and the loan's governing law. This lesson teaches how a lawyer reads each, explains conditions subsequent, material adverse change and cross-default, and compares in concept how Canada and Guyana approach enforcement.
body:
A construction loan is a set of conditional promises. Your rights depend on exactly how each condition and each default is worded, how strictly a court in the governing jurisdiction would read it, and what the lender must do before enforcing. Words that look routine decide who controls a half-finished building.

Recall

Q. What does equity first cost a developer in return terms?

A. It ties equity up longer before completion, which lowers the internal rate of return even when profit and the equity multiple are unchanged, partly offset by lower interest.

Q. What is the qualified transferee test in an intercreditor agreement?

A. The definition, usually by experience and net worth, of who may take ownership of the borrower if a junior lender enforces.

Q. What is the purpose of a geotechnical desk study before buying land?

A. To identify ground risks, such as poor soils or a high water table, from existing records before committing, so foundations and cost are not a surprise.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender rarely refuses to fund by saying no. It says a condition is not satisfied, or that an event of default has occurred. Whether it is right depends on wording you approved months earlier. What follows teaches concepts and how to think, not the law of any particular jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the loan's governing law, and in the law where the land sits if that is different.

Is the commitment letter binding?

In week 20 we learned that whether a preliminary document binds depends on intention, certainty of terms and the language used. A commitment letter usually binds the lender to lend if, and only if, every condition is satisfied by the expiry date. Some letters go further and bind both sides to proceed in good faith; others are so qualified, with phrases such as "subject to satisfactory documentation" and "subject to final credit approval", that they promise little. The professional reading question is: what exactly could the lender rely on to walk away? Every subjective condition, phrased as "satisfactory to the lender in its sole discretion", is a door the lender can use.

The first worked example. Two commitment letters each require "a construction contract satisfactory to the lender". Letter A adds "in its sole discretion". Letter B says "on substantially the terms of the draft contract dated 1 March, with any material changes acceptable to the lender, acting reasonably". Under letter A, a lender that has changed its mind about the market can reject a perfectly ordinary contract. Under letter B, it can reject only material changes, and only for reasons that are reasonable. Same condition, different promise.

Conditions subsequent and how conditions are read

A condition precedent must be met before the lender acts. A condition subsequent is a requirement the borrower must satisfy after funding, by a stated date, such as registering a security document or delivering a final title policy within 30 days of closing. Missing it is usually an event of default, so a condition subsequent turns a closing item into a deadline. Lenders sometimes agree to move a condition precedent that is late into a condition subsequent so that closing can proceed. That helps, but it converts a delay into a default risk, so it must be tracked as carefully as the original.

Say that out loud now.

Material adverse change and cross-default

A material adverse change clause lets the lender refuse to fund, or call a default, if something significantly worsens the borrower, the project or sometimes the market. Courts in many common law jurisdictions have tended to read these clauses narrowly, requiring a change that is significant and lasting rather than a temporary dip, but how any particular clause would be read depends on its wording and the governing law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The drafting points that matter are whether the clause covers general market conditions or only the borrower and project, whether it requires the lender to act reasonably, and whether it applies only as a condition to drawing or also as an event of default.

Cross-default, which Ford took apart this week, comes in two strengths. Cross-default is triggered when another debt is in default, even if that other lender has done nothing. Cross-acceleration is narrower: it is triggered only when another lender has actually demanded repayment. Borrowers negotiate for cross-acceleration, for a threshold amount below which other debts are ignored, and for the clause to reach only the borrower, not every company the sponsor owns.

After an event of default

The second worked example follows a default through the documents. In month 14 of a hypothetical 22-month build, the borrower misses a monthly report deadline. The loan agreement gives 10 business days to cure a reporting default. On day 12 the report is still missing. An event of default has occurred. The lender may now refuse further draws, which is its immediate remedy and the one that matters most during construction. It may also accelerate: declare the whole loan due. Then it may enforce its security: appoint a receiver to take control of the project, or step into the construction contract under the direct agreements it signed with the contractor and the architect. Each step depends on notice provisions being followed exactly. Many loan agreements require written notice to specific addresses; a remedy exercised without proper notice can be challenged.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source for both countries before relying on it. In Canada, property and civil rights are largely provincial, so the remedies available to a mortgage lender, including power of sale, judicial sale and foreclosure, and the steps and timelines each requires, differ from province to province, and Quebec follows its own civil law framework. The appointment of receivers over a debtor's business is also shaped by federal insolvency legislation. Guyana's legal system rests on a common law foundation, with its own legislation on mortgages, land registration and companies, and its own court procedures for enforcing security. For a construction loan in Guyana, the questions to put to counsel are which remedies a mortgagee has without going to court, how long a contested enforcement typically takes, how security over company shares and project contracts is registered and ranked, and whether a loan denominated in a foreign currency raises any additional requirement. The concept is the same in both places: the lender's practical power over a half-built project depends on how fast and how cleanly it can enforce, not on the size of the loan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting subjective conditions and broad default triggers because they look standard, then meeting them in month 14 with the building half finished. The control is to have your lawyer mark every condition the lender can judge in its sole discretion and every default without a cure period, and to negotiate each to an objective test or a reasonable-lender standard before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the event of default list as a list of disasters. Most items are administrative: a late report, a lapsed insurance certificate, a missed condition subsequent. These are the defaults that actually happen, so they need the longest cure periods.

Callback

In week 25 we learned to instruct lawyers in writing and to ask what would change their advice. Here that discipline pays directly: instruct counsel to list every subjective condition, every default without cure, and every notice requirement, and to report how each would likely be read under the governing law.

Recap

A commitment letter binds only as far as its conditions allow, and every sole-discretion condition is a door out for the lender. Conditions subsequent turn closing items into deadlines. Narrow the material adverse change clause, prefer cross-acceleration with a threshold, and make sure every administrative default has a cure period and proper notice.

Next: Priya with the numbers: a worked test of conditions precedent and covenants through a build, step by step.
checklist: Mark every condition the lender may judge in its sole discretion
Negotiate each to an objective test or reasonable-lender standard
List every condition subsequent with its deadline and owner
Narrow the material adverse change clause to the borrower and project
Ask for cross-acceleration, a threshold amount and borrower-only reach
Give every administrative default a cure period
Confirm notice addresses and procedure for every default
Professional sign-off required: lawyer in the governing law and where the land sits
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the rules of construction lending in one minute. A commitment letter binds the lender only as far as its conditions allow, and every condition judged in the lender's sole discretion is a door out. A construction contract satisfactory to the lender in its sole discretion is a weak promise; one on the terms of a dated draft, with material changes acceptable to the lender acting reasonably, is a strong one. A condition subsequent must be met after funding by a date, and missing it is usually a default. Material adverse change clauses should cover the borrower and project, not the whole market. Cross-acceleration, with a threshold and borrower-only reach, is better than full cross-default. After a default, the lender's first remedy is to stop funding, then accelerate, then enforce, and every step depends on proper notice. Enforcement differs by province in Canada and has its own path in Guyana, so counsel must confirm both.
terms: Condition subsequent — a requirement the borrower must satisfy after funding, by a stated date, failing which a default usually occurs.
Material adverse change — a clause allowing a lender to refuse funding or declare a default if the borrower's or project's position worsens significantly.
Cross-acceleration — a narrower form of cross-default, triggered only when another lender has actually demanded early repayment.

hostile.q: Our standard form says satisfactory to the lender in its sole discretion. Why should we change it?
hostile.a: Because it lets you decline to fund a project you have already approved, for reasons unrelated to the project. I am not asking you to give up protection. I am asking that the contract condition be on the terms of the draft you have reviewed, with material changes acceptable to you acting reasonably. That protects you against a changed project without making the commitment worthless to me.

title: Testing a construction loan's conditions and covenants, step by step
summary: A worked calculation takes a hypothetical construction loan from commitment to month 20: the equity test before the first draw, a pre-leasing condition, a cost increase that changes the equity requirement, and a schedule slip against the outside completion date. Units are stated at every step.
body:
The conditions and covenants of a construction loan are arithmetic before they are law. Run them as numbers at commitment, at first draw and every month after, and you will see a breach months before the lender writes to you about it.

Recall

Q. What is a condition subsequent?

A. A requirement the borrower must satisfy after funding, by a stated date, failing which a default usually occurs.

Q. In the capital stack, what is cumulative coverage?

A. Net operating income divided by the combined cash cost of a layer and every layer senior to it.

Q. How is residual land value calculated?

A. Finished value minus all costs minus the required profit; what remains is the most the project can pay for the land.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the lender's monitor and credit team will run these numbers every month. If you run them first, you choose how to respond. If you do not, the lender chooses for you. All figures are hypothetical, and the ratios and requirements are commercial practice that varies by lender, not standards.

Step 1: the commitment

A hypothetical rental building has a total budget of 30,000,000 dollars, including land at 5,000,000, hard costs of 19,000,000, soft costs of 3,500,000, finance costs of 1,500,000 and contingency of 1,000,000. The commitment letter offers 65 percent loan-to-cost: 0.65 multiplied by 30,000,000 is 19,500,000 dollars of loan. Equity is the balance: 30,000,000 minus 19,500,000 is 10,500,000 dollars. The conditions to first draw include: equity spent in full, pre-leasing of at least 30 percent of rentable area, the permit issued, and a fixed-price construction contract. The outside completion date is month 24 from first draw.

Step 2: the equity test before first draw

By the date you plan to request the first draw, your cost report shows spending of 9,200,000 dollars: the land, design fees, permits and the first months of site work, all paid with equity. The lender will not fund until equity spent reaches 10,500,000. The shortfall is 10,500,000 minus 9,200,000, which is 1,300,000 dollars. You must either spend another 1,300,000 of your own money on eligible costs first, or contribute it into a lender-controlled account that will be spent before the loan. The planning lesson: forecast the month in which equity spending reaches the required figure, and set the first draw date there, not earlier.

Step 3: the pre-leasing condition

The building has 100,000 square feet of rentable area. Thirty percent is 0.30 multiplied by 100,000, which is 30,000 square feet. You have signed leases on 27,000 square feet and a letter of intent on another 5,000. Most lenders count only signed leases, often only those meeting minimum term and rent conditions, so your qualifying figure is 27,000 square feet: 27 percent, 3,000 square feet short. A letter of intent does not count. You need one more signed lease of at least 3,000 square feet, or a waiver from the lender. Start that conversation now, with the letter of intent in hand, rather than at the first draw meeting.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: a cost increase

In month 6 the structural package comes in 1,200,000 dollars over its budget line. The contingency of 1,000,000 is not untouched contingency any more; part of it has already been committed. Many loans require the project to stay in balance: the undrawn loan plus any remaining equity must be enough to finish. Assume the lender will not increase the loan. Then the new total cost is 30,000,000 plus 1,200,000, which is 31,200,000 dollars, and the loan stays at 19,500,000. Required equity becomes 31,200,000 minus 19,500,000, which is 11,700,000 dollars: 1,200,000 more than planned, contributed before the lender's next draw. Loan-to-cost falls to 19,500,000 divided by 31,200,000, about 62.5 percent. The lender is safer; you are 1,200,000 poorer in liquidity. Week 40 takes this in-balance test further.

Step 5: the schedule against the outside date

The baseline schedule shows completion in month 22 from first draw, leaving two months of float before the outside date of month 24. At month 14, the monitor reports the work is three months behind. The forecast completion is now month 25: one month past the outside date. That will be an event of default in month 25 unless an extension is agreed.

Calculate your options. The commitment letter allows one extension of three months on payment of a fee of 0.25 percent of the commitment: 0.0025 multiplied by 19,500,000 is 48,750 dollars. The extension also requires no other default to be continuing, so check the reporting and insurance covenants now. Alternatively, accelerating the work to recover a month might cost, say, 300,000 dollars in overtime and extra crews. The extension is cheaper, provided its conditions can be met. Ask for it in month 14, in writing, with the recovery schedule, while you are still in compliance, not in month 24 when you are not.

Step 6: interest during the delay

A three-month delay also costs interest. If the loan averages 15,000,000 drawn in the final months at a hypothetical 8 percent, that is 15,000,000 multiplied by 0.08 divided by 12, or 100,000 dollars a month, about 300,000 for three months. If the interest reserve was sized to month 22, it now runs short by about three months, which itself may put the loan out of balance. Delay costs twice: in interest and in the covenant test that interest triggers.

Step 7: the summary table

Put the results on one page: equity shortfall 1,300,000; pre-leasing shortfall 3,000 square feet; extra equity from the cost increase 1,200,000; extension fee 48,750; extra interest about 300,000. Total cash the developer must find, beyond the original plan: about 2,850,000 dollars, of which 1,300,000 is timing and the rest is real cost. That table is what you take to your investors and your lender, before they ask.

Step 8: testing the plan against the commitment expiry

One more test belongs on the same page, because it comes first in time. Suppose the commitment letter was signed on day 0 and expires on day 150. The CP tracker shows the permit expected on day 120, the construction contract signed on day 100, the final signed lease for the missing 3,000 square feet expected on day 135, and the equity shortfall of 1,300,000 spent by day 140. The latest item is day 140, which leaves 10 days before expiry. Ten days is thin: one late item and the commitment lapses, and a renewal may come with a fee or worse terms. The professional response is to ask, now, for an automatic 30-day extension of the commitment on payment of a small fee, and to start the lease negotiation immediately so it is not the last item on the tracker. Every condition has a lead time, and the tracker turns those lead times into a single number: the days of margin before the promise expires.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is meeting each condition and covenant one at a time, as a surprise, rather than seeing their combined demand on your cash. The control is a monthly covenant and condition test, run by you, with the cumulative cash requirement at the bottom.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts a letter of intent towards a pre-leasing condition and plans the first draw on it. Lenders count signed, qualifying leases. Plan on those alone.

Callback

In week 13 we built sources and uses and learned that contingency is a budget line, not spare money. This calculation shows why: the moment contingency is consumed, a construction loan's balance test turns the next overrun into new equity from you.

Recap

Size the loan and the equity at commitment. Forecast when equity spending meets the requirement. Count only qualifying leases. Turn every overrun into new equity in the balance test. Compare the schedule with the outside date monthly and ask for any extension early. Total the cash demands on one page.

Next: LEX in the room: negotiating the commitment letter's conditions, cure periods and outside date with the lender and its counsel.
checklist: Calculate loan and equity from the loan-to-cost limit
Forecast the month equity spending reaches the requirement
Count only signed leases that meet the lender's tests
Recalculate required equity after every overrun
Compare forecast completion with the outside date every month
Price any extension and confirm its conditions now
Calculate extra interest from any delay and test the interest reserve
Total all extra cash demands on one page
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, testing a construction loan in one minute. A 30,000,000 dollar budget at 65 percent loan-to-cost gives 19,500,000 of loan and 10,500,000 of equity. With 9,200,000 spent, I am 1,300,000 short of the equity the lender requires before its first draw. The pre-leasing condition needs 30,000 square feet signed; I have 27,000, and a letter of intent does not count. A 1,200,000 overrun with no loan increase raises my equity to 11,700,000 and lowers loan-to-cost to about 62.5 percent. A three-month delay moves completion to month 25, past the outside date of 24; a three-month extension costs 48,750, far less than accelerating, but only if no other default is continuing. The delay also adds about 300,000 of interest. Total extra cash: about 2,850,000. I put that on one page before anyone asks.
terms: Pre-leasing condition — a requirement that a stated share of the building be leased under qualifying signed leases before the lender funds.
Outside completion date — the latest date by which the borrower must complete construction without being in default.
Extension fee — a fee paid to a lender to extend a date in the loan, such as maturity or the outside completion date.

hostile.q: You are three months behind at month 14. Why should we grant the extension?
hostile.a: Because I am asking while every covenant is in compliance, with a recovery plan the monitor has reviewed. Forecast completion is month 25 against an outside date of 24. I will pay the 48,750 extension fee, top up the interest reserve by 300,000 from equity now, and report against the recovery schedule fortnightly until completion.

title: In the room: negotiating the commitment letter
summary: A realistic meeting with a construction lender's relationship manager and its counsel to settle the commitment letter. The lines to say about conditions, cure periods and the outside date, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state when counsel says a clause is standard.
body:
The commitment letter is negotiated in one or two meetings and then lived with for two years. The aim is not to win every clause; it is to remove the clauses that would let a lender walk away from a project that is going to plan.

Recall

Q. Why does a cost overrun usually become new equity under a construction loan?

A. Because the loan must stay in balance, and if the lender will not increase the loan, the remaining cost can only be covered by more equity from the borrower.

Q. What is the difference between cross-default and cross-acceleration?

A. Cross-default is triggered when another debt is in default; cross-acceleration only when another lender has actually demanded repayment.

Q. In the capital stack, why can a mezzanine lender act faster than a senior lender?

A. Because a pledge of the shares in the borrowing company can often be enforced faster than a mortgage over land, and taking the company brings the building with it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the lender's counsel drafts the commitment letter, and its first draft protects the lender against everything it can imagine. Most of that protection costs you nothing. A few clauses cost you everything if they are used. Your job is to know which few, and to spend the meeting on them.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are closing a hypothetical 19,500,000 dollar construction loan. Around the table: Mr Osei, the lender's relationship manager, who wants the deal done; Ms Grant, the lender's counsel, who wants it done safely; and your own lawyer. You have marked five clauses in advance: the construction contract condition, which is in the lender's sole discretion; a material adverse change clause covering general market conditions; cross-default reaching every company you own; reporting defaults with no cure period; and an outside completion date of month 24 with no extension right.

The lines to say

Open with the bottom line and a short list: "I am ready to sign this week. There are five points, and none of them changes your economics. Each one is about making sure you cannot be forced, or tempted, to stop funding a project that is on plan." That framing invites Mr Osei to help, because a stalled loan is bad for him too.

On the contract condition: "Your team has reviewed the draft contract dated 1 March. I am asking that the condition be that contract, with material changes acceptable to you acting reasonably." On market conditions: "If the market worsens, your protection is the pre-leasing condition and the balance test, which you already have. A market-wide adverse change clause lets you stop funding a building whose leases and budget are intact." On cross-default: "Limit it to this borrower, with a threshold of, say, 250,000 dollars, and to acceleration rather than default." On reporting: "Ten business days to cure any reporting or administrative default. The defaults that actually happen are late paperwork." On the outside date: "Month 24 against a 22-month schedule is two months of float. I want one three-month extension, at a fee, available if there is no payment default."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "we will never need it" about a cure period or extension. If you will never need it, it costs the lender nothing to give it, and you have signalled you have not planned for delay. Never say "every other lender agreed to this." Ms Grant knows what other lenders agree to, and you will be asked to prove it. Never accept "it is standard" as an answer by repeating it back; ask instead, "Standard for what risk?"

The question behind the question

When Ms Grant says "we need sole discretion on the contract because it is the biggest risk in the deal", the question behind it is "how do we know you will not sign a weak contract after we commit?" Answer that: "You will see the final contract before closing and can reject material changes. If I want to change the contractor, that is a change of the condition, and you can say no." When Mr Osei asks "how confident are you in the 22 months?", he is asking whether you understand your own schedule. Answer with the critical path and its biggest risk: "The structural frame is the critical path. The steel is ordered and the fabricator's slot is confirmed in writing. Weather in the second winter is the risk, and the extension covers it."

When to stay silent

When counsel offers a compromise, such as a five-business-day cure instead of ten, do not answer at once. Pause, write it down, and look at your list. The pause is not theatre; it gives you time to check whether five days is actually workable for your reporting cycle. If it is, accept it plainly. If it is not, say why in one sentence. Silence is also the right response to the relationship manager's small talk about how keen the credit committee is. That is pressure dressed as warmth.

How to hold your state

Lawyers negotiating for a lender often use a calm, slightly bored tone that makes your requests sound unusual. Do not match it with urgency. Match it with the same calm. Before the meeting, write your five points and, for each, your fallback: the minimum you would accept. If you are told twice that a clause is non-negotiable, take it to the relationship manager privately after the meeting: what will credit actually accept? A commercial question to the commercial person often unlocks what a legal question to the lawyer cannot.

Reading the outcome

The worked result. The contract condition moves to the dated draft with a reasonable-lender standard. The market-wide adverse change clause is narrowed to the borrower and the project. Cross-default becomes cross-acceleration, borrower only, with a 250,000 threshold. Reporting defaults get five business days, which your lawyer confirms is workable with a monthly report due on the fifteenth. The extension is granted at a fee of 0.25 percent, 48,750 dollars, conditional on no payment default. Mr Osei asks in return for monthly rather than quarterly cost reports. You agree: it costs you a little effort and gives the lender earlier warning, which is exactly what the cure periods depend on.

The second check is your own arithmetic: with a 22-month schedule, the outside date of 24, and the extension to 27, you now have five months of protected float against a two-month float before. That is the single most valuable change in the meeting.

Send a short written summary of every agreed point the same afternoon, so the next draft is prepared from your list rather than from memory.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is spending the meeting on the interest rate or legal fees and leaving the walk-away clauses untouched. The control is a written list of the clauses that let the lender stop funding a sound project, settled one by one before any economic point is reopened.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to win every redline and exhausts the goodwill needed for the five that matter. Concede the ones that cost you nothing, early and visibly.

Callback

In week 3 we studied reciprocity: people tend to return a concession. Giving the lender monthly cost reports without argument was not weakness; it was a deliberate concession on a point that costs you little, made in exchange for the extension, which is worth a great deal.

Recap

Arrive with your five clauses marked and a fallback for each. Frame every request as protecting a project that is on plan. Answer the question behind the question with evidence. Pause before accepting a compromise. Take refusals to the commercial person. Trade cheap concessions for valuable protections.

Next: Kema closes the week with six questions, a Red Pen drill on a commitment letter, and a boardroom explanation of construction lending.
checklist: Mark the clauses that let the lender stop funding a sound project
Write a fallback position for each marked clause
Open by stating you are ready to sign and listing the points
Ask for objective or reasonable-lender standards on every condition
Narrow cross-default to borrower-only cross-acceleration with a threshold
Secure cure periods for administrative defaults
Secure an extension right at a fee on the outside date
Concede low-cost requests early in exchange for protection
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the commitment letter meeting in one minute. I arrive with five clauses marked: the construction contract condition in the lender's sole discretion, a market-wide adverse change clause, cross-default reaching all my companies, reporting defaults with no cure, and an outside date with no extension. I open by saying I am ready to sign and none of my points changes the lender's economics. I ask for the dated draft contract with a reasonable-lender standard, the adverse change clause narrowed to the project, borrower-only cross-acceleration with a threshold, cure periods for paperwork, and a three-month extension at a fee. I never say we will never need it. I pause before accepting a compromise. I trade monthly cost reports, which cost me little, for the extension, which is worth a great deal. The result: five months of protected float instead of two.
terms: Relationship manager — the lender's commercial lead on a borrower's account, responsible for winning and maintaining the business.
Fallback position — the least favourable outcome on a single point that a negotiator has decided in advance to accept.
Float — the time by which an activity or a whole schedule can slip without breaching a fixed date.

hostile.q: Our counsel says the sole-discretion contract condition is standard. Why should we move?
hostile.a: Standard for protecting you against a changed project, and I am happy to give you that protection. I am asking you to tie the condition to the draft contract your team has already reviewed, with material changes subject to your reasonable approval. That protects you completely against a weaker contract and removes only the right to refuse a contract you have already accepted.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 39 review: construction lending from term sheet to default
summary: Six questions on commitment letters, conditions precedent, covenants and events of default, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical commitment letter extract with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a construction lender promises to fund only while its conditions are met and no default has occurred, so the developer's real work is turning every condition into a dated task and every default into a cure path.

Recall

Q. What is float in a schedule?

A. The time an activity or the whole project can slip without breaching a fixed date, such as the loan's outside completion date.

Q. In a waterfall, what does the catch-up do?

A. After investors receive their preferred return, the catch-up gives the sponsor a larger share of the next distributions until the sponsor has its agreed percentage of total profit to date.

Q. What is an intercreditor agreement?

A. A contract between lenders to the same project setting out payment priority, enforcement rights, standstills, cure rights and consents.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a review turns knowledge into a reflex you can use in a meeting. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What does a commitment letter promise? Answer: That the lender will fund on stated terms if every stated condition is met by the expiry date. It binds only as far as its conditions allow, and every sole-discretion condition is a way out for the lender.

Question 2. Name three sets of conditions precedent in a construction loan. Answer: Conditions to closing, such as authorisations, title and security; conditions to the first draw, such as the permit, the construction contract, pre-leasing or pre-sales and equity spent in full; and conditions to every draw, such as no default continuing and the loan in balance.

Question 3. Why does equity first lower IRR even when profit is unchanged? Answer: Because the equity is invested earlier and stays tied up longer before completion, partly offset by lower interest since debt is drawn later.

Question 4. What is a condition subsequent, and why does it matter? Answer: A requirement to be met after funding by a date. Missing it is usually a default, so it turns a closing item into a deadline.

Question 5. In the worked test, why did a cost overrun of 1,200,000 become new equity? Answer: Because the lender would not increase the loan and the loan had to stay in balance, so required equity rose from 10,500,000 to 11,700,000.

Question 6. What is Rule 39? Answer: I never fund a long build with debt that matures or can be called before the project can repay it, and I map every cross-default so that one failure cannot pull down the rest.

Say that out loud now.

Week recap

Day 1 traced the three documents and the three families of terms: conditions precedent, covenants and events of default. Day 2 took Dubai World apart and found a maturity mismatch and unwritten support. Day 3 priced fees, equity first and delay. Day 4 read conditions, material adverse change and cross-default as a lawyer would, and compared enforcement in concept across Canada and Guyana. Day 5 ran the conditions and covenants as numbers. Day 6 negotiated the five clauses that let a lender walk away.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical commitment letter extract and find the defects before reading on.

Facility: 19,500,000 dollars, being 65 percent of total costs of 29,000,000. Expiry: this commitment expires 60 days from the date of this letter. Conditions to first draw: building permit issued; construction contract satisfactory to the Lender in its sole discretion; pre-leasing of not less than 30 percent of rentable area, including leases and letters of intent; Borrower equity of 10,500,000 contributed. Events of default include any default by the Borrower or any affiliate under any indebtedness of any amount; any failure to deliver a report when due; any material adverse change in market conditions. Outside completion date: 24 months from first draw. No extension.

The defects. First, the arithmetic: 65 percent of 29,000,000 is 18,850,000, not 19,500,000, so either the cost or the loan is wrong, and the equity figure of 10,500,000 only works with a 30,000,000 budget. Second, a 60-day expiry is almost certainly shorter than the permit and contract timeline; it must be tested against the CP tracker. Third, the sole-discretion contract condition gives the lender a way out after commitment. Fourth, counting letters of intent towards pre-leasing is unusual and, if the lender later reads the clause strictly, the developer may be relying on leases that do not qualify; get the definition written precisely. Fifth, cross-default covers any affiliate and any amount: one small debt anywhere in the group could stop funding. Sixth, no cure period for reports. Seventh, a market-wide adverse change clause. Eighth, no extension right on the outside date.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Try it now, aloud, then compare with this model answer.

Model answer: "We have a commitment for a 19,500,000 dollar construction loan, 65 percent of a 30,000,000 budget, with 10,500,000 of our equity going in first. The commitment runs 150 days, which covers the permit timeline with a month to spare. Before the first draw we need the permit, the fixed-price contract on the draft the lender has reviewed, 30 percent pre-leasing on signed leases, and our equity spent; each item has an owner and a date. During the build we must report monthly, keep the loan in balance, and complete by month 24, with one three-month extension available at a fee. Defaults are limited: cross-acceleration applies only to this borrower above 250,000, and paperwork has a cure period. Our biggest exposure is a cost overrun, which becomes new equity, so we hold a further 1,500,000 in reserve outside the project."

Score yourself

Record your two-minute answer and score it 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: were the loan, equity and dates right? Structure: did you open with the commitment and its expiry? Composure: steady pace, a pause after each key number? The hard question: did you say what happens if costs rise?

Where you will meet this again

In week 40 the draws, the interest reserve and the in-balance test turn this week's conditions into a monthly routine, and the guarantees arrive. In week 41 pre-sale thresholds replace pre-leasing as the key condition for a condominium.

A practice habit for the week ahead

Take any commitment letter or term sheet you can find, real or hypothetical, and spend fifteen minutes doing three things. List every condition to the first draw with a plausible lead time and see whether the expiry date survives. Mark every clause the lender could judge in its sole discretion. And find the cross-default clause and write down, in one sentence, which other debts could trigger it. Speed at those three tasks is what lets you answer a lender's draft in a day rather than a week.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a commitment that cannot be used because its conditions cannot be met in time, or that can be withdrawn on a clause nobody read. The control is a CP tracker and a marked list of walk-away clauses before signing.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the commitment letter as the finish line. It is the start of a second negotiation that ends at the first draw.

Callback

In week 20 we learned that conditions and remedies decide what a contract really does. This week applied it to the most consequential contract a developer signs: every condition is a door, every default is a remedy, and the wording decides who holds the keys.

Recap

Track every condition backward from the first draw, negotiate dates against a sober schedule, narrow the walk-away clauses, map every default to a cure path, and match every maturity to a delayed timeline.

head: The six questions
speak: Mr Shabazz, week 39 in sixty seconds. A construction lender funds a building that does not exist, so it protects itself with conditions. The term sheet binds almost nothing; the commitment letter promises funding if conditions are met by a date; the loan agreement sets conditions precedent, covenants and events of default. I build a CP tracker backward from the first draw. Dubai World showed the danger of a maturity mismatch and of cross-default, giving Rule 39: no debt that matures or can be called before the project can repay it, and every cross-default mapped. Fees, equity first and delay can cost more than a quarter-point of rate. Sole-discretion conditions and market-wide adverse change clauses are doors out for the lender, so I narrow them. Every overrun becomes new equity under the balance test. And in the room I spend my time on the five clauses that let a lender walk away.
terms: Commitment letter — a lender's written undertaking to lend on stated terms subject to stated conditions and an expiry date.
Covenant — a continuing promise by the borrower in a loan agreement to do, or not to do, something while the loan is outstanding.
Cure period — the time allowed after a breach for the borrower to fix it before it becomes an event of default.

hostile.q: Your summary says 65 percent of 29,000,000 is 19,500,000. Which number is wrong?
hostile.a: The cost. The budget is 30,000,000, which gives 19,500,000 of loan and 10,500,000 of equity; 29,000,000 was the budget before contingency was added. I will have the commitment letter corrected so the loan-to-cost limit and the equity requirement are calculated on the same approved budget, because a mismatch there becomes an equity dispute at the first draw.
